solutionText:

solutionText:

pawns, but they are weak defenders against pawn storms, and White’s plan is to attack on the
kingside. Larsen won after: 24...Rea7 25.Bg5 Ra1+ 26.Kh2 R8a2 27.Qf5 Ne6 28.Bh4 Rf1?!

material loss to a pawn. 28...Qxf7 29.Rd1±  Exchanging on f7 would have helped the black
king to e6, and forced c3-c4 to win back the piece. And that would have left the b4-pawn en
prise. The opposite-coloured bishops give Black drawing chances, but fortunately White can keep
the rooks on in order to make better use of his advantage.

If the queen moves, Black wins back the exchange with ...Bc8 and/or ...Nd2. 23.Bc7!  Qa8
The only try. 24.Qh3 24.Qd7 is also clearly better. 24...Re7± 24...Bc8 25.Qf3± is no longer a

This exercise is about making a decision, and avoiding a tempting sacrifice. 14.Bg5! Bringing the
bishop into the attack in the most effective way. Two alternatives: a) 14.g4 looks winning and is
winning, even though Black gets some counterplay with 14...d5. White chooses between 15.Ba2
dxe4 16.dxe4 Qd4 17.g5 Bxe4 18.Ne2!+– and 15.g5 g6 16.fxg6 fxg6 17.Qg4+– (full points for
both choices on move 15). b) 14.Bxh6?! gxh6 15.Qxh6 Bg7 16.Qg5 Nc6! The only way to defend
against 17.f6, but now White’s best is to exchange queens. That’s disappointing, even though
White still has a strong attack after 17.Nd5! Qxg5 18.hxg5±. 14...d5 14...hxg5? 15.hxg5  with
mate next move. 14...Nc6 defends the bishop but Black’s pawn structure will nevertheless suffer

22.Kh2 Qg2 mate  21...Re6 Threatening 22...Qg5+ 23.Kxh3 Rh6+ mating. Black’s attack is
winning (0–1, 56 moves). Opening the files will soon decide the game after: 22.f4 g5–+

26...Qb7? Easily winning, right? 27.c6! Don’t underestimate a passed pawn! 27...Qxb2 28.Qxb2
Or 28.Rd8+ Nxd8 29.Qxb2. 28...Rxb2 29.Rd8+! A standard motif with a pawn on the sixth
rank versus a knight. 29...Nxd8 29...Kh7 30.Rxa8+– 30.c7+– Both promotion squares cannot
be protected. 30...Rb1+ 31.Nf1 Rd1 32.c8=Q Bb7 33.Qc2 Rd5 34.Nxg6 1–0 So Black should
have avoided the tempting mating threat. Stronger was 26...Nxd4= .

37.Nh5! Some other moves also win, but the winning idea is still this move. 37...gxh5 38.Qh6 
Preparing 39.Nf6 mate. 38.Rg3+ Bg4 39.Qh6 also works. 38...f6 39.Qg6+ Kh8 40.Nxf6 1–0
Black is mated, as he also would be after other moves.

324 The Woodpecker Method

game: Alexander Khalifman – Grigory Serper, St Petersburg 1994
solutionText:
27.Bxd7! 27.Nxe5 Qxe5² counterattacking the b2-rook. There is no way to win after 27.d6
cxd6. 27...Nxd7 27...Rxd7 can be met by, among others, 28.Nxe5 28...Qxe5 29.Qxd7+– 
and if Black tries to save the knight with the lifeline 27...Qxd7, White threatens b7 and then
picks up the knight on e5. It can be done in three ways: 28.Rcb5+– , 28.Qb4+– or 28.Qb3+–.
28.Rxb7+! 28.Rxc7!? Kxc7 29.Qxa7 Rb8 30.d6+ also wins after 30...Rxd6 31.Rxb7+ Rxb7
32.Qxb7+ Kxb7 33.Nxd6+ Kc6 34.Nxe8. But 28.Rcb5?! Nb6 is only an advantage. 28...Kxb7
29.Rxc7+! Kxc7 30.Qxa7+ Kc8 31.d6  1–0 Mating next move.

17...Bh3! The fork on f3 decides. 18.Qc2 18.gxh3 Nf3+–+ ; 18.Nf4 Bxg2! 19.Nxg2 Nf3+–+ 
18...Bxg2–+  (0–1, 27 moves)

Several lines might win slowly, but the easiest is 39.Nf5+! Kg6 40.Rxg7+!+–  and the fork on
e7 leaves White two pawns up in an endgame.

18.Ne4!  18.Ng4 Qd8 19.Qc3± 18...fxe4 18...Qd8 19.Ng5+! with a winning attack
(or various other moves with a winning position anyway). 19.fxe4 Nf4 20.gxf4 Or first 20.Bd6+–.
20...Rhd8 21.Bd6+– White is dominating and won the game. Weaker is 21.fxe5?! Rxd2±.

16.c6! The fork on e7 wins a piece or allows the pawn to queen. 16...Qa7 16...Nxc6 runs into:
17.Qxc6! Qxc6 (17...Bxd5 18.exd5+–  or 18.Qxd5+–) 18.Nxe7+ Kh8 19.Nxc6+–  17.c7!
Bxd5 17...Nd7 18.Nxe7+ Kh8 19.c8=Q+–  18.c8=Q+–  (1–0, 36 moves)

 Solutions to Intermediate Exercises 325

game: Michael Unger – Alexander Khalifman, Bad Wiessee 1998
solutionText:
30...Bxf2+! 31.Kg2 31.Kh1 Qf1 mate and 31.Rxf2 Qxe4 wins the queen. 31...Be3+!  Black
takes the bishop on the next move (0–1, 44 moves). But 31...Qxe4+ 32.Rxe4 Bc5µ is not over
yet.

30.f5! Opening an additional file for the decisive breakthrough. 30...exf5 31.Rg1! Nf4 31...Rg8
32.Bxg6+ Rxg6 33.Re7++–  was the point of opening the e-file before playing Rg1. 31...Rxe3
32.Bxg6+  wins for White. 32.Bxe8+–  With such a useless bishop as the one on d7, Black
really cannot claim compensation (1–0, 72 moves).

30...Rxg2+! 30...axb6 31.Nb5! and the queen can’t keep the pin on the f-pawn while defending
the knight on d2. However, Black is clearly better after 31...Qg4 32.Qxg4 Rxg4 but unlike
the game, White can fight on. And if 30...Nf3+? 31.Kf1 Rxg2 he has an equal position after
32.Qxf3! Rxf3 33.Rxd4. 31.Kxg2 Qg7+! 32.Kh2 32.Kh1 Rh3 mate  32...Nf3+ 33.Qxf3
33.Kh1 Qg4!  mating. 33...Rxf3–+  White resigned in two more moves.

40.Rxc5! 40.Nc7?? Qxc7 41.Rxc5 Qxc5 42.Qxf7+ Kh6–+ 40...Qxc5 41.Qf6+ Kg8 41...Kh6
42.Re4+–  (or 42.Ne3+–) 42.Ne3!+–  Black cannot defend against the onslaught without
taking heavy casualties. 42.Nf4!+– is even cleaner, and 42.Nb6 wins as well, even though it sends
the knight in the wrong direction. Instead the game went 42.Ne7+?? Rxe7 43.Qxg6+ when
White had nothing better than a perpetual, since the rook on d8 defends against rook lifts.

33...Nxd5! White collapses on the light squares, incurring heavy material losses. 33...Rxf3
34.Kxf3 Nxd5+ 35.Ke2 Qxe6 36.exd5µ is also a good try, but not clearly winning. 34.Rf2
34.exd5 Qxf3+–+  34...Bxc6 Not the easiest win. 34...Ndf4+–+ is one good move, 34...Ne3+
another. 35.Qxh6 35.exd5 requires Black to find: 35...Rxf3! 36.dxc6 (36.Rxf3 Qxf3+ [or
36...Bxd5–+] 37.Kxf3 Bxd5+ 38.Kg4 Bxh1–+) 36...Rxf2+! 37.Bxf2 Qxe6 This is winning, since
38.Qxh6? runs into 38...Nf4+–+. 35...Qxe6?! Now Black starts to drift. Better is 35...Ne3+
36.Kh2 Qxe6 winning. 36.exd5 Bxd5 37.Bxd5 Qxd5+ 38.Kh2 Black should still win, but
there are difficulties, and in the game he did not play accurately enough (½–½, 62 moves).

solutionText:
19...Neg4+! 19...Nfg4+ 20.Kg1 Nxe3 21.fxe3µ is less convincing, as here the knight would be
better on f6 because of the control over e4 and pressure on e3. 20.hxg4 20.Kg1 Nxe3 21.fxe3 
The e3-pawn can be taken at will, so Black is much better. 20...Nxg4+ 21.Kg1 Bxg2 22.Kxg2
Rxe3!µ  The rook cannot be taken, so Black has won a pawn for no compensation. White
collapsed quickly: 23.Nf4 Rd8 24.Rh1 Re4 25.Rc1 Nxf2 0–1 Another tactic against the white
king and queen finished the game. 26.Kxf2 is met by 26...Rxd4 27.Qxd4 Bb6 winning the
queen.

326 The Woodpecker Method

game: Alexander Khalifman – Ilya Duzhakov, St Petersburg 2012
solutionText:
24.e4! Driving away the defender of the bishop on d6. 24.g4? hxg4 25.hxg4 Bxd5 26.Rxd5
Nh4 is not winning – White needs e4-e5. 24...Ng7 24...Bxc5 25.exf5+– wins a piece, which
is preferable to 25.bxc5 Ng7 26.Nf6++– winning the queen. 25.Nxe7+! Bxe7 25...Qxe7
26.Bxd6+–  26.Rxd8+–  (1–0, 29 moves)

29...f2! Clearing the way for the queen to do serious damage. 29...Qxg5 30.Bf2 is equal. 30.Bxf2
Qxf2 31.Rxh1 Qf3+ 32.Kc2 Qxh1µ  Black has a healthy pawn extra, and won after 41 moves.

20.Nxc6! There are three tempting options that don’t work: a) 20.Ne6?? Nxe6–+; b) 20.Nf5??
Nxf5–+; c) 20.Qxg7+? Kxg7 21.Nf5+ Kg8 22.Nxh6 mate is nice, but the opponent is seldom so
helpful. 21...Kg6 22.Nxe7+ is also good for White, but 21...Kf7 22.Nxd6+ Ke6 leaves Black a
piece up. 20...Qxg4 20...Rf7± and White has won an important pawn. 21.Nxe7+ Kf7 22.hxg4
Kxe7 Instead Black tried 22...Nd3 but his position was hopeless after 23.Nf5 (1–0, 26 moves).
23.Bxg7  With so many extra pawns, White is winning.

 Objectivity consists in understanding that the only one who never

solutionText:

Or 33.Qd6. 33...Qg6 34.Qd8+ 1–0 Black resigned due to 34...Qg8 35.Qxf6+ Qg7

30.Bxf6 Bxf6 31.Re7+! Sacrificing an exchange to win on the dark squares. 31...Kh6 31...Bxe7
32.Rxe7+ Kh6 33.Qd4 Rg8 34.Qf6  delivers mate, while the d-pawn decides after 31...Kg8
32.Rc7  (32.d7 is also winning). 32.Rf7! Still going for the dark squares. 32...Bh4 33.Qd4!

35...g5 36.Rf6+ Bg6 37.Rxg6+ Kxg6 38.Re6+ Kf5 39.Qf7 mate

usually much stronger than a rook and pawn.

in one way: 28.Bd8+! Rxd8 29.Qe6+ Kg5 30.Nf3+ Kf4 And now there are several ways to mate

after 40.Qxg4 or 40.Rd3. 39.Bg6+ Kf8 40.e7+ Qxe7 41.Bxe7+ Bxe7 42.Bd3!+–  This is the
only winning move, preventing the black counterplay connected with ...Rd2+, while keeping a
rook that it is needed in the attack (1–0, 45 moves).

game: Vladimir Kramnik – Magnus Carlsen, Monte Carlo (rapid) 2007
solutionText:
22.Rc6! Somewhat weaker is: 22.Qh7 Ke7 23.Rc6! Rxc6 (23...Nd7 24.Qh4+!+–) 24.Qxg8 Rc8
25.Qh8+– and 22.Raa6 Ke7 (22...Nxa6? 23.Rxe6++–) 23.Rac6 Rxc6 24.Rxc6 Qxb5 25.Rxc5+–.
22...Rxc6 Instead the game ended after 22...Nd3 23.Rxc8+ Qxc8 24.Rxa7 1–0 23.bxc6 Qxc6
24.Qh8 Black doesn’t have a second rook on the back rank any more. Also 24.Qh7+– is good
enough. 24...Rxh8 25.gxh8=Q++–

32...Nce3? A tempting but bad try that Kramnik fell for. 32...Qf8µ  is best, but anything other
than the main line that does not seem bad gives full points. Two more alternatives are 32...Bxf2+
33.Qxf2 Rxc6 34.Bxc6 Qxc6³ and 32...Nfd6³. 33.fxe3 Nxe3 34.Bd4! 34.Rd2 Nd5+ 35.Kh1
Qxc6 with a winning position, was Black’s idea. 34...Bxd4 35.Rxd4 35.Nxd4? Nxd1 36.Qxd1 is
winning for Black due to the two pawns and White’s unstable knight. Nxg2 36.Nb4!= The knight
on g2 is trapped, so Black will have to show some care to draw this with some pawns for a knight.

24...Nf2! Black’s tactical threat is 25...dxe4, but the knight might also just continue to d3. Not
24...dxe4? 25.Qxc4+±. 25.Be3!? A smart try, but not good enough. 25...Nd3!  Black threatens
the rook but also 25...Ba6 followed by 26...dxe4. White’s knight can’t move due to a discovered
attack. Worse is: 25...Bxe3?! 26.Rxe3 Nd3 27.Rxd3 Bxd3 28.Qxd3 dxe4 29.Bxe4µ 26.Re2 Nb4
0–1

328 The Woodpecker Method

29.Nxd4?? Take a full point for any non-blundering move, but best seems either 29.Nd2÷ or
29.Bxd7÷. 29...Qxd4 30.Rd1 Nf6! 31.Rxd4 Nxg4 32.Rd7+ Kf6 33.Rxb7 Rc1+ 34.Bf1
Maybe White had seen this far and counted on his queenside pawns to decide the game, but it

22...Bxg2! 22...Qg4? 23.Ng3= 23.Ng3 23.Kxg2 Qh3+  is mating. For example: 24.Kg1
Qh1+ 25.Kf2 Qf3+ 26.Kg1 Rh1 mate 23...Bf3!  Black has plenty of pawns for the piece, and
a winning attack. Or 23...Rh4!? 24.Qxg2 Rxf4–+. 24.Qb3 After 24.Nxh5 Nxh5–+ White’s king
is naked and Black’s troops are incoming (or 24...Qg4+). 24...Rh4 25.Bd6 Qh3 26.Bxf7+ Kh7
27.Qb2 Ng4 0–1 Mate is coming.

Black is clearly better, but has a way to break through right now. 30...Nxf2! 31.Kxf2 Qc2+
32.Kg1 32.Kf1 Qd3+ 33.Kf2 Qe3+ does not help White. 32...Qd1+ 33.Kf2 33.Kg2 Qe2+
34.Kg1 Qxf3–+  33...Qxh1–+  0–1

22.Rxa6! Rxa6 23.Qxd3 A double threat. 23...Qxb2 23...Qa8 24.Qxe2+–  24.Rb1 Rd6
25.Qxe2+–  The game ended swiftly: 25...Qa2 25...Rxd2 26.Rxb2 Rxe2 27.Rxe2+– 26.Qb5
c6 27.Qb2 1–0 White’s two pieces and the passed a-pawn are much stronger than a rook and
c-pawn.

29.Nd5! Opening up the way to the king. 29...exd5 30.Bxf6+–  1–0 Threatening Ng7+, and
the bishop cannot be taken due to mate. Black chose to resign since trying to create an escape
square does not help: 30...Nb8 31.Bg7 Qe7 32.Nf6+ White wins the queen and the game.

37.Bh6! Threatening 38.Rb8+ Be8 39.Qg6+. Other moves are better for White, but this is the
only winning move. 37.Rb8+ Kg7 38.Bh6+? even loses: 38...Kxh6 39.Rh8+ Kg5–+ 37...Nc7
37...f5 38.Qa1!  Qc3 (38...e5 39.Qxe5 Qxh6 40.Rb8++–) 39.Qa8+! This is the difference
between placing the queen on a1 and b2. White wins after 39...Kh7 40.Qf8!. 38.Qb4! The
game continued 38.Ra7 which is also winning: 38...Nb5 39.Qb4 Nd6 40.Qb8+ Ne8 41.Re7+–
(1–0, 51 moves) 38...Kh7 39.Qf8+– Black has to give up the bishop on f7 to avoid mate.

35.Rg1! Instead, the game continued 35.Bxf8?! exf1=Q+ 36.Rxf1 Rxg2 37.Qxg2 Bxg2+
38.Kxg2 Rxf8² (½–½, 60 moves). White is also slightly better after 35.Bg5 exf1=Q+ 36.Rxf1
Rxg2 37.Qxg2 Bxg2+ 38.Kxg2 Bh6. 35...Bxh6 Black also loses after 35...exd1=Q 36.Qxd1! 
with a double threat and 35...e1=Q 36.Rdxe1 Rxg2 37.Qxg2! (37.Rxg2?? Rxe1 mate) 37...Bxg2+
38.Kxg2.  36.Rde1+–  The material advantage is large enough to win.

26.Ne6! A nice discovery/closing tactic. Either the king is mated or the queen is lost. 26.e6 is not
the way to go: 26...Bxe4 27.Qxf7+? (27.exf7+ Kh7 28.Bxe4 Bxd4 29.Bxg6+ Kh8 30.Bb2 e5=)
27...Kh8–+ But 26.Rg4!? Qxa2 27.Bb2+– is also quite strong. 26...Bxe6 26...Bxe4 27.Qxf7+
Kh7 28.Qxg7 mate  27.Rxc4+–  (1–0, 30 moves)

The bishop on c7 has a nice line of sight to the white king, so Black just needs some smart
sacrifices to make full use of it. 22...Nxh3! 23.gxh3 Rxf3–+ White can’t take back: 24.Qxf3?!
e4  And the queen has to go.

solutionText:

to h6 decides the game; Black tried to prevent the immediate threats, but to no avail. 33.Bxa1

21.gxf3 Nd3 22.Bxf8± 19.Bxd8 Rxf1+ 20.Kxf1  I believe White should win with correct

solutionText:

solutionText:
38...d5!! 38...Ke6? 39.b5+– was played in the game. 39.cxd5 39.b5 dxc4 40.bxa6 c3 41.a7 c2
42.a8=Q c1=Q±  and the a-pawn is far advanced, but Black should have sufficient counterplay.
39...Ke5! Or 39...Ke7. 40.dxc6 Kd6 41.Kf3 Kxc6 42.Kg4 Kb5 43.Kxg5 Kxb4 44.Kh6
Kxa5 45.Kxh7 Kb4 46.g4 a5 47.g5 a4 48.g6 a3 49.g7 a2 50.g8=Q a1=Q²  A theoretical
draw.

15.Bxe7! It is possible to start with 15.Bxh7+, but 15.Bf4 Ncxd3 16.cxd3 f6 17.Nxe5 fxe5
18.Bxe5± only gives a positional advantage. 15...Nxf3 16.Rxf3! Qxe7 17.Bxh7+! Kxh7
18.Rh3+ 18.Nf5 transposes or wins the queen after: 18...Qg5 19.Rh3+ Kg6 20.Rg3+– 18...Kg8
18...Kg6 is obviously suicidal: 19.Qh5+ Kf6 20.Rf1 mate. 19.Nf5! Qg5 20.Qh5! 1–0 The end
could have been: 20...Qxh5 21.Ne7+ Kh7 22.Rxh5 mate

21.Rd5!! 21.Rc2 g6!³ and White has to fight to show his compensation. Even worse is
21.hxg7? Rxd2 22.Rh8+ Kxg7 23.Rh7+ when Black can run to e7 or sacrifice the queen:
23...Kxh7 24.Qh5+ Kg8 25.Qxg5+ Ng6 26.Qxa5 Rxf2–+ 21...Rxd5 21...cxd5? 22.Qxe5 gxh6
(22...f6 23.Qxe6+ Rf7 and White has many winning moves. One that requires little calculation
is 24.h7+ Kh8 25.Qxf7+–.) 23.Rxh6 (or 23.Nh5, mating) 23...f6 24.Qxe6+ Rf7 25.Nh5!+–
The pawn on f6 falls and it’s Game Over. 22.cxd5 Qxd5 22...Ng6 does not really defend the
king after: 23.hxg7 Kxg7 24.Nh5+ Kg8 25.Qf3! f5 26.Qe3+– 23.hxg7 Kxg7 The game was
agreed drawn here. 24.Nh5+ Kg6 25.Nf4+! gxf4 26.Qh5+ Kf6 27.Qh4+ Kf5 28.Qh5+ Ke4
28...Kf6 29.Qh4+= 29.Qe2+=  It’s a perpetual, since Black cannot allow Rd1+ winning the
queen.

39.Nxf7! 39.Bxg6? fxg6 40.Nfxe6+ looks tempting, but Black has 40...Kg8 41.Rxf8+ Qxf8 and
the knight is pinned, forcing White to find the clever 42.Nh7! Rxh7 43.Qxg6+ Rg7 44.Nxf8
Rxg6 45.Nxg6 to be only clearly worse. 39...Rxf7 39...Qxf7 40.Nh5++–  White takes the
queen and then crashes through on g6. 40.Nxg6! Rxg6 41.Qxg6+  White picks up the
h4-pawn and will be at least clearly better, although that evaluation is not so easy to make.
41...Kf8 42.Rxf7+ Qxf7 43.Qh6+ Qg7 43...Ke7 loses to 44.Bg6+– and 45.Qxh4+. 43...Kg8!
is best, since the king keeps control over the h8-square. White is winning on the kingside after
44.Qxh4, but Black has some hope to get the d4-pawn. 44...Qe7!± tries to exchange the defender.
44.Qxh4+–

356 The Woodpecker Method

21.Nxg7! There are a lot of alternatives, but none are as strong: a) 21.Qg3?! Qg5! 22.Rg4 Qe3+²
b) 21.Rg4 g5! 22.fxg6 Bxg4 23.gxf7+ Nxf7 24.Nf6+ Kg7 25.Nxg4± c) 21.f6?! g6² 21...Ne4 The
main point is 21...Kxg7 22.f6+ Kh8 23.Qh4  with a winning attack. 22.Bxe4 22.Rxe4 Rxe4!±
and White is a pawn up, but has less of an attack than in the main line. 22...Rxe4 23.f6+– White
has won a pawn and Black’s king is quite exposed. It should be enough to win.

 Tigran Petrosian
 They say my chess games should be more interesting. I could
 be more interesting – and also lose.

White is an exchange up and will win back the trapped queen by a rook check on d7. 40.Rd7+!
The game was agreed drawn after 40.Qxh7? Nxh7 41.Rd7+ Qxd7 42.cxd7. Opposite-coloured
bishops favour the player with an active position, which is Black in this case. He will use his
kingside majority and has full compensation after 42...Bg7. 40...Qxd7 40...Nxd7 41.Qxh7+– 
and the pawn on e5 drops. 41.Rxe5+ If the king moves, White takes on f8 with check, so the
following moves are forced. 41...Qe6 42.Rxe6+ fxe6 The queen is still trapped on h8, but will be
resurrected by pawn promotion. 43.c7! Rxh8 44.c8=Q  White picks up the queenside pawns
and should be winning.

12.Nxf7! 12.g4?! Bg6 13.h4 Bxe5 14.dxe5 a4 15.Bc4 Nb6³ and the pawn on c2 is en prise.
12...Kxf7 13.g4! White didn’t win any material, but he did open the light squares around Black’s
king. 13...Qf6 Black can’t move the bishop: 13...Bg6? 14.Qxe6++– , and 13...a4 leads to the
same fate: 14.gxf5 axb3 15.Qxe6+ Kf8 16.Qxd6+±  14.gxf5±  White’s advantage with his
light-squared bishop and safer king is significant (1–0, 72 moves).

36.g5! Nf5 a) 36...fxe5 37.Qf6+  Kg8 38.Rh1 is mating. b) 36...f5 37.Qh3+– and the h-file
decides (other moves also win, but more slowly). c) 36...Ng8 37.gxf6+ Nxf6 38.Rxc6+– with
a winning attack. d) 36...fxg5 37.Qf7+ Kh8 38.Rh1 mate  37.gxf6++–  37.Qf4+– is also
strong enough. The game move gives a decisive attack. 37...Kxf6 38.Rxc6+ Ke7 39.Qf4 1–0
The attack will yield further dividends.

28.Qh6+! a) 28.d8=Q? Rxd8 29.Qxd8 and White is lost on the queenside, but seems able to fight
well enough on the dark squares for a draw. Black can play: 29...Ne2+ 30.Rxe2 Qd1+ 31.Kh2
Bxg2! 32.Kxg2 Qxe2= b) 28.Qe7? Raa8–+ c) 28.gxf3? Rxd7–+ d) It is possible to start with
28.Rxc3 and follow up in the same way, but it allows 28...Qxd4 when the h8-square is defended,
although White is still winning. 28...Kg8 29.Qxf8+! 29.Bg5? Qxd4³ 29...Kxf8 30.d8=Q+ 
Kg7 31.Bh6+! There are other winning moves. 31...Kh7 31...Kxh6 32.Qh8 mate 32.Qf6! 1–0
Mate is coming.

 Solutions to Advanced Exercises 357

20...Nxe4! Using the back rank and the light squares weakened due to White missing his light-
squared bishop. 21.Nxe4 Bf5! White would likely have resigned here. Instead 21...Rf1+ was
played and brought a swift victory; it should be winning, even against a tougher defence than
was played, but the main line is stronger. 22.Kc2 Bf5 23.Qg2 (a better defence is 23.Rxc4
Rc8 24.Qd3 although White is in trouble after 24...Ra1!–+) 23...Qh4 (or 23...Qa5–+) 24.Rxc4
Qe1!–+ Black has a winning attack (0–1, 29 moves). 22.Qc2 Qh4! 23.Rxc4 Rac8 White is
overloaded. 24.Nf3 Rxc4 25.Nxh4 Bxe4–+  Black is a rook up.

White is clearly better anyway, but also has the chance to force a direct win. 32.Rxd8+! Kxd8
33.Qb8+ 33.Bxe6 Qc2+ 34.Kf3 Qc6+ and White has to exchange queens and give up the
f-pawn. Black can fight for a while after 35.Qe4 Qxe4+ 36.Kxe4 Nxf6+ 37.Ke5 Ke7 38.Bh3.
33...Qc8 33...Kd7 34.Qxg8+–  34.Qxc8+ Kxc8 35.Bxe6+!+– The bishop will take all three
pawns, since it cannot be taken due to f6-f7-f8=Q.

White can force the pawn through with some accurate moves. 35.e7! 35.Qf4+?! Kc8 (35...Kb6²)
36.Rg8+ Rd8² 35...Re5 35...Ra5 36.Qf4+! Kd7 (36...Kb6 37.Qb4+ Ka6 38.Qxa5++– )
37.e8=Q+ Kxe8 38.Rg8+  The king is checked upwards and Black has to give up the queen to
avoid mate. 36.Qg7!+– Two threats: against the rook, and to queen with a discovered check. Not
36.Qf4? Qd6=. 36...Kd6 37.Qxe5+  1–0

Black has put his faith in the rolling e- and f-pawns winning the dark-squared bishop to keep his
king out of danger. 31.Nf3! Making room for the crucial minor piece to get out of danger and
onto the a1-h8 diagonal. Not 31.Bxe4 fxe3 32.Nf3 Rxf3 and Black is not much worse. 31...exd3
White also wins after other moves: 31...exf3 32.Bd2!  followed by 33.Bc3, 31...fxe3 32.Nxe5 
and 31...Qf6 32.Bd4 . 32.Qxd3!  Instead White went for 32.Nxe5? dxc2 33.Bd4! dxe5
34.Bxe5+ Kh7 35.Rg7+ Kh8, but Black had too much counterplay with the pawn on c2, so
White had to make a draw: 36.Rf7+ Kg8 37.Rg7+ Kh8 38.Rg6+ Kh7 39.Rg7+ ½–½ 32...Bf5
33.Qe2 33.Nxe5 (33.Bd4 Bxd3 34.Nxe5 transposes) 33...Bxd3 34.Bd4! also wins: 34...dxe5
(34...Be4+ 35.Nf3+!+–) 35.Bxe5+ Kh7 36.Rg7+ Kh8 37.Rxc7+ Kg8 38.Rg7+ Kh8 39.Rxa7+
Kg8 40.Rg7+ Kh8 41.Rg3+ Kh7 42.Rxd3+– All the pawns for the exchange will decide.
33...fxe3 34.Nxe5 exf2 35.Rg2 35.Rf1 is also good. 35...Be4 36.Ng6+ Bxg6 37.Rxf2+–

358 The Woodpecker Method

game: Bent Larsen – Tigran Petrosian, Santa Monica 1966
solutionText:
24.Qh6! Threatening 25.Bxe6 or 25.Rh3. 24.Rxf6? exf6µ gets White nowhere. 24...Bg7
25.Qxg6!! 25.Qh4? is not even a repetition: 25...f5µ 25...Nf4 a) 25...Nc7 is a double threat,
but Black gets no time to execute it: 26.Qxg7+! Kxg7 27.Rg5+ Kh6 28.Rh3 mate  b) 25...fxg6
26.Bxe6+ Kh7 (26...Rf7 and White can transpose to the main line with 27.Rxf7 or get a winning
attack after 27.Bxf7+ Kf8 28.Bxg6+ Bf6 29.Rh5) 27.Rh3+ Bh6 28.Bxh6 Rf5 29.Rxf5! gxf5
30.Bf7!+–  The threat of 31.Bf8 mate is hard to defend against. White could have captured the
f5-pawn first, but there’s no point. 26.Rxf4! fxg6 27.Be6+  Rf7 27...Kh7 28.Rh4+ is the same
as 25...fxg6 26.Bxe6 Bh6. The only difference is that Black can try 28...Bh6 29.Bxh6! g5 when
both moves win: 30.Bxg5++– and 30.Rxg5 Qb6+ 31.c5!+–. 28.Rxf7+– It’s over. Also strong is:
28.Bxf7+ Kf8 29.Bxg6+ Bf6 30.Rh5+– 28...Kh8 28...Be5 29.Rf5+ Kh8 30.Rfxe5+– 29.Rg5!
b5 30.Rg3 1–0

game: Tigran Petrosian – Heikki Westerinen, Palma de Mallorca 1968
solutionText:
28.f5! hxg5 a) 28...Bxf5? 29.Bxf6! Rxe2 30.Qd8+ (or 30.Bxe2+–) 30...Qf8 31.Qxf8+ Kxf8
32.Bxg7+ (White has two other winning moves: 32.Bxe2 and 32.Rd8+ Re8 33.Bxg7+ Kxg7
34.Rxe8+–.) 32...Kxg7 33.Bxe2+– b) 28...gxf5 29.Bxh6+–  and White is a pawn up, while
Black’s structure and king’s position are in ruins. 29.fxe6 Rxe6 30.Rxe6  fxe6 31.Qxg5
White is winning, being a pawn up while Black has many weaknesses and no counterplay
(1–0, 41 moves).

28.Nc6! 28.Qe5!? maintains a serious advantage. 28...Qd6 29.Qxd6 Nxd6 30.Rc7! and White is
probably winning. But 28.Re8? Qxd4–+ should be avoided. 28...Nd6 29.Nxd8! a) Just as good
is: 29.Ne7+! Kh8 30.Ng6+! Kg8 (30...fxg6 31.Qxf8+ Rxf8 32.Rxf8+ Kh7 33.d8=Q+–) 31.Nxf8
Nxf5 32.Rxd8 Qxd8 33.Re8+– White enjoys an extra rook after spending a tempo to create luft
for the king. b) 29.Rxd8 Rxd8 30.Nxd8 Nxf5 and White only wins an exchange. However, that’s
enough after the precise 31.Nb7! Kh7 32.d8=Q Qxb7 33.g4!+– when the knight is caught.
29...Nxf5 30.Nc6  1–0 White queens with an extra rook left on the board. 30.Nb7 would
have been similar.

34...Rxd3! Black is clearly better and probably winning after simple moves, such as 34...a3 or
34...R3c4, but no points for such cowardice this time! 35.Rxd3 Qxf2+ 36.Kh2 36.Kh1 Ng3+
37.Kh2 Nf1+ 38.Kh1 Nxe3 is straightforward. 36...Qg3+ 37.Kg1 Material is now equal, but
Black wins with a fork on f2. 37...Qf2+ Spassky starts with a repetition. 38.Kh2 Qg3+ 39.Kg1
Nf2!–+  Black captures the pawn on h3, with an ongoing attack.

 Solutions to Advanced Exercises 359

33.Nxe4! 33.Bf3 Be5+! (33...exf3? 34.Nxf3 creates a double threat of Rxg6 and Bxd8. Black
is still fine materially, but White’s initiative is winning.) 34.Kh1 Qh6= 33...fxe4 34.Bxe4 Qe6
 a) 34...Be5+ 35.Kh1 Qe6 threatens mate, so White has to postpone taking on d8. 36.Re3!+–
Black can’t defend against 37.Rg6 (or 36.Rg4+–).
 b) 34...Qh6 35.Bg5! allows the queen to reach h4. After 35...Qe6 36.Qh4!  Be5+ 37.Kg2!
Black must give back the piece: 37...Qxh3+ 38.Qxh3 Bxh3+ 39.Kxh3+– Black is lacking
coordination: the knights are on the edge, the rook on d8 is threatened and the king can come
under attack. And White is also a pawn up.
 c) 34...Qf7 35.Bxd8 Rxd8 and White has a winning attack; strongest seems 36.Rxg7! Kxg7
37.Rf2 Qe6 38.Qc3+ Nf6 39.Qg3+ Ng4+ 40.Qxg4+ Qxg4 41.hxg4 with a winning endgame.
35.Rxg7! The only winning move in a complicated position. The game continuation 35.Re3? was
considered strong by Petrosian in his commentary on the game, but with a computer we can see
that it is not the strongest continuation: 35...Rde8 36.Be7 Qe5+! (to prevent Qc3+ after ...Bh6)
37.Kh1 Bh6 and things are not so clear. 35...Kxg7  35...Nxg7 36.Bxd8 Rxd8 37.Qh4++– 
After the king captures on g7, there are different ways to continue the attack, usually leading
to a won endgame. However, it’s enough if your intuition evaluated this position as winning.
36.Bxd8 a) 36.Rg2+ Kh8 37.Qc3+ Rf6 (37...Nf6 38.Rg6 Qxh3+ 39.Qxh3 Bxh3 40.Bxf6+
Rxf6 41.Rxf6+–) 38.Bxf6+ Qxf6 39.Rg5+– b) Or first 36.Qc3+ Rf6 37.Rg2+ Kh8 38.Bxf6+
Qxf6 39.Rg5+–. 36...Rxd8 37.Rg2+ Kh8 37...Kf8 38.Bd5! Qxe1 39.Rg8 mate 38.Qc3+! Qf6
38...Nf6 39.Rg6 Rf8 (39...Qxh3+ 40.Qxh3+ Bxh3 41.Rxf6!+–) 40.Rh6+ Kg7 41.Rh7+ Kg8
42.Qg3+ Ng4+ 43.Qxg4+ Qxg4 44.hxg4+– 39.Rg5! Qxc3 40.Rxh5+ Kg7 41.bxc3+–

game: Tigran Petrosian – Yuri Balashov, Soviet Union 1974
solutionText:
21.Qe4! Bringing the queen into the centre to attack the light squares (g6 and e6). Not
21.Bxf7+? Kxf7 22.Qc4+ Kg7µ. 21...Kg7 21...Bxg5 22.Qxg6+ Kf8 23.Qxg5+–  22.Bxf7!
Kxf7 23.Bh6! Cutting off the king’s retreat, threatening Qe6/c4/d5+ with a devastating attack.
23...Qd6 a) 23...Nd4 defends against queen checks, but White is easily winning after 24.Qxd4.
b) 23...Bf6 24.Qc4+ Re6 25.Qxe6 mate  c) 23...Nd8 24.Ne5+ with mate. 24.Qc4+! Kf6 
White’s attack is so strong that several moves win. 25.Rad1 25.Ng5!+– with threats against f7
and h7. 25...Nd4 26.Qxd4+ Qxd4 27.Rxd4+– Rc5 28.h4 1–0

25.Nf6+! Bad are 25.Bxd5? Rxd5 26.Rxd5 Nb4–+ and White cannot play 27.Rc5, and 25.Rxd5?!
Rxd5 26.Bxd5 Nb4 27.Bc4 Nd3µ. 25...Kh8 25...Bxf6? 26.exf6 Qxf6 (26...Qf8 27.Rxd5 Rxd5
28.Bxd5 Nb4 and the difference compared to the immediate capture on d5 is that the bishop
on b7 is undefended: 29.Bxb7! Rxc1 30.Rxc1+–  White will win the queen back, with an extra
piece.) 27.Bxd5 Rxd5 28.Rxd5 Nb4 29.Rc5  With the queen no longer on e7 this defence is
possible, with a winning material advantage. 26.Nxd5  White is clearly better, although Black
won the game (0–1, 41 moves).

23.Rxf7! Thanks to some nice geometry, White picks up some material and a good position.
23.Qxg6 Nxc3 24.Nxd6+ Bxd6 25.Rxd6 Ne2+ 26.Kd1 Ra6 is unclear. 23...Rxf7 24.Qg8+ Rf8
24...Bf8? 25.Nxe4 Bxe4 26.Nxd6++–  25.Qxg6+ Kd7 26.Nxe4 Bxe4 27.Qxe4±  White
has three pawns for the exchange and a safer king (1–0, 38 moves).

360 The Woodpecker Method

36.Ne4! Attacking the blocker on f6. Not 36.Nxe6? Qxe6 37.Bc4 Qxc4 38.Rxc4 Re1 mate.
36...Nd7 White is certainly happy after this retreat, so you don’t have to see further. After
36...Rf7, the way for White to break through is to win the e6-pawn with the bishop. 37.Bc4
(or similarly 37.Nxf6+ Nxf6 38.Bc4) 37...Ng4 (37...Qb2 38.Nxf6+! [38.Bxe6? Ra1 39.Nxf6+
Kh8! 40.Rf1!= with a perpetual] 38...Nxf6 39.Bxe6 Ra1 and White has enough resources to win
material and defend against the perpetual: 40.Bxf7+ Kxf7 41.Qxh7+! Ke8 [41...Ke6 42.Re3+
Kd5 43.Qf7+ Kd6 44.Qe7+ Kd5 45.Qe5 mate ] 42.Qxg6+ Kd7 43.Rf1 The queen can come
back to c2 to defend against checks.) 38.Qg5!  White has too many threats for Black to parry.
(38.Qh4?? Qxc4!µ turns the game around, but 38.Bxa2 Nxh6 39.Bxe6+– is good enough.)
36...Nxe4 37.Rf8 mate  37.Qg5! Many moves are winning, for instance 37.Bc4 first or 37.Nc5
going for the f8-square. Ivkov played the slightly cautious 37.h3?! but perhaps it was time trouble,
and the win was spoiled a few moves later. 37...Rf7 38.Bc4 Qb2 39.Bxe6+–

 Boris Spassky
 A man who is willing to commit suicide has the initiative.

27.Nxe4! Not 27.Qxe3? Qxh4+ 28.Kg2 Bxf4–+, nor 27.Rxg7? Rxf4–+. 27...Rg6 The point of
the knight sacrifice is that White threatens mate after 27...Rxe4 28.Rxg7. Black can try 28...Qxg7
29.Rxg7 Kxg7 but is mated after: 30.Qg1+! (30.Qg3+ also wins, but allows 30...Kf7 31.Bxf6
Nf5) 30...Kf7 31.Bxf6 (31.Bh5++– is not as strong, but still good) 31...Kxf6 32.Qg5+ Kf7
33.Bh5+! Kf8 34.Qf6+! Kg8 35.Bf7+  Kf8 36.Bg6+ Kg8 37.Qf7+ Kh8 38.Qxh7 mate.
27...Rxf4 is met most easily by 28.Qxf4 Bxf4 29.Bxg7+ Qxg7 30.Rxg7 since Black can’t take on
e4. 28.Nxd6 Vvedensky lost after 28.Rh5? Qxf4! because 29.Qxf4 Rxg1+µ comes with check.
28...cxd6 29.Rh5 The queen is trapped and cannot escape after trading on g1 due to Qxg7 mate.

21.Nxe6! fxe6 It is difficult to find a clear-cut win, but as Black’s king cannot castle short or long,
there should be something. You can actually chose between three winning moves. 22.Qg4! I think
this is most clear-cut, but other moves are also winning. a) 22.Qc4 Qb6 23.Qxa4+ transposes to
22.Qxa4+. b) Spassky played 22.Qxa4+ when 22...Qb5 23.Qg4 was similar to 22.Qg4. If Black
had defended with 22...Ke7 the best way is 23.Qh4+ Ke8 24.Qg4+– with the same position as
22.Qg4, but without the pawn on a4. It is a little greedy to spend energy on that, but still full points,
of course. 22...Qc6 Black has two other ways to try to defend. a) 22...Qe7 deprives the king of its
only square: 23.Qxa4+ is mating. b) 22...Rf8 23.Qxe6+ Be7 24.Rxf8+ Kxf8  25.Rd7 wins the
queen with a winning material advantage, or 25.Rf1+ with a winning attack: 25...Ke8 26.Qf7+
Kd7 27.Rd1+ Kc6 28.Qe6+ Kc5 29.Rd7+– 23.Qxg7 Rf8 24.Rxf8+ Bxf8 25.Qxh7+– 
Black has no active moves, and no defence against 26.Qg6+ Ke7 27.Rd6 Qc8 28.Qf6+ Ke8
29.Rxe6+.

 Solutions to Advanced Exercises 361

game: Boris Spassky – Lothar Zinn, Marianske Lazne 1962
solutionText:
24.Nxf7! Kxf7 24...Nxd6  25.Nxd6+– does not win back the exchange straight away (Black
can pin the knight), but with 26.Qe5 to come, Black collapses. 25.Bxe6+ Or 25.Rxe6. 25...Qxe6
26.Rxe6 Kxe6  Black has enough material for the queen, and he would be fine if he had time
to return his king to safety. But that dream will not come true. It’s fine to evaluate this position
intuitively. 27.Qb3+ Ke7 27...Kf6 28.e5+!+– 28.Qg8! 29.Bg5+ is a threat. 28...h6 29.Rd6!
Precise, but other moves were also winning. 29...Nxd6 30.cxd6+ Kd7 31.Qf7+ It is also possible
to start with 31.Qxg7++–. 31...Kxd6 32.Bf4+ Kc5 33.Qf5++– The rook on c8 is collected.

20...a5! Not a beautiful combination, but that doesn’t make it any less strong! 21.dxe4 Black’s
idea is: 21.bxa5 Bb2 22.Qa4 Be2!³  Only like so. Black has serious threats against both d3
and f1. And not 22...Bxc1?! 23.Rxc1 with compensation for the exchange. 21...Be2!µ A precise
move, winning an exchange since the bishop coming to c4 spells trouble for the c5-knight due
to the undermining of b4 that was commenced by 20...a5!. 21...axb4 22.Qb3 Ra3! 23.Qb1
Bc3 is also advantageous for Black. 22.Qb3 Tougher is giving up the exchange with: 22.bxa5
Bxf1 23.Rxf1 Bb2 24.e5! Bxa3 25.exd6 Bxc5 26.dxe7µ 22...Bc4! 23.Qb1 axb4 24.Bxb4 Bxa2
Weaker is 24...Bxf1 25.Bxf1µ. 25.Nd3 Bxb1 26.Bxd6 Bxd3–+ (0–1, 48 moves)

35.d6! There is still some work left after 35.Rxb8 Rxb8 36.Ba5 Rd8! 37.Bxc7 Rxd5±. 35...Ra8!?
35...Rxb5 fails to 36.dxe7 Rxc5 37.exd8=Q++–  and 35...cxd6 36.c7 Rxb5 37.cxd8=Q+– 
is another route to a new queen. 36.dxe7 Ra1+ 37.Be1  37.Ke2 Ra2+ makes no progress.
37...Rdd1 38.g3 The threat of promoting to a queen instead of a knight prevents the ...g6-g5-g4
idea, leaving White with a winning endgame. Instead Spassky won after the spectacular but
weaker 38.e8=N+?! Kf7! 39.g4± (39.g3 g5! forces White to give a perpetual due to the dangerous
attack on his king) 38...Rxe1+ 39.Kg2 Kxe7 40.Rxe5++–

26.Nxd6! Judging this as too dangerous to play and instead going for a normal move would be a
reasonable practical decision (1 point). 26...e4! 26...Qxd6 27.Qxf5+–  is simple. 27.Nxe4! Ne5!
28.Nxc5! 28.Qe2? Nxe4 29.Qxe4 Nxf3+ and Black wins. 28...Qc8 28...Nxd3 29.Nxd7+– 
White will retain two extra pawns. 29.Qd4! Hodgson played 29.Qe3? and resigned after
29...Nfg4 30.Qd4 Nxh2!. White is mated after 31.Kxh2 Rh5+ 32.Kg1 Qh3. 29...Nxf3+
30.Rxf3 Rxf3 31.Ne6!²  The knight stops Black’s queen from joining the attack. It is so
strong that Black most likely should give up an exchange for it, simultaneously destroying White’s
central domination. White should remain slightly better. Other moves than 31.Ne6 would make

game: Veselin Topalov – Miguel Illescas Cordoba, Linares 1995
solutionText:
20.Nc7! White creates threats against d6 and e6, and the black bishop can’t hold both d5 and f5.
20...exf4 White is not afraid of a sacrifice: 20...Rxg3+ 21.hxg3 Qxg3+ 22.Ng2+–  A better try is
20...Bc4!? 21.Nxf5 (21.Nxc4? exf4! with an initiative) 21...Rxf5, but White seems to be winning
after 22.Bxf5. 21.Ng2! Qh3 21...Qe7 22.Nxe6 Qxe6 23.Bb3+–  22.Rxf4! A necessary move
to make the combination sound. Instead 22.Nxe6? fxg3 23.hxg3 Be3+! completely turns the
tables: 24.Rf2 (24.Nxe3 Qxg3+ 25.Kh1 Qh3 mate) 24...Bxf2+–+ Also misguided is: 22.Nxf4?
Bxf4 23.Rxf4 Rxg3+ 24.hxg3 Qxg3+ 25.Kh1 Qh3+ 26.Kg1 Rf6µ 22...Bxf4 22...Rxc7 23.Rh4+–
23.Nxf4 Rxg3+  24.Kh1!+– Wherever the black queen moves, White can play 25.Ncxe6 with
a winning position (and there are also other good moves). 24.hxg3?! may be slightly better for
White after 24...Qxg3+ 25.Ng2 Ne5! 26.Nxe6 Nf3+ 27.Qxf3! Qxf3.

solutionText:
29...Bb5! 29...Qa6 30.Qd2= 30.R2e3 30.Re1 Rxb3! 31.axb3 Bd3+–+  30...Rf2–+  The
threats of ...Qc6, ...Bd3+ and ...Rcc2 are too much to handle for White in conjunction with
the resource ...Rf1+ in some situations. 30...Rf1+? 31.Re1 is only unclear. The game move is
also acceptable: 30...Bd3+ 31.Ka1 Qxd4?! (stronger is 31...Rf2! 32.Re1 Rxb2! 33.Kxb2 Rc2+
34.Ka1 Qc6!–+ with a double threat: ...Qc3 and ...Qg2) 32.Rxe6 Rf1+ 33.Re1 Black has a large
advantage (0–1, 54 moves).

21.Nxe6! Rxe7 21...fxe6 22.Rxd7±  22.Nxg7! Qb7!? A double threat against f3 and g7 (since
the knight on d7 is protected). 22...Kxg7 23.Rxd7! (the move order 23.Qg4+ Bg6 24.Rxd7
runs into 24...Rxe3 or 24...Qc8) 23...Rxd7 24.Qg4+ Kh8 25.Qxd7  Regaining the rook,
when the two healthy pawns extra and his safer king leaves White winning. 23.Bd4!+– 
Pinning the e4-bishop so that ...Bf3 is not possible while simultaneously protecting the g7-knight.
Here too, White is two pawns up for no compensation. 23.Qg4 Bf3 24.Qh4 Rxe3 25.Nf5 is a
good try, but Black can defend with 25...Re6 26.Qg5+ Rg6÷ and things are not so clear.

27...Bc2!!–+ Clearing a path to f2 with tempo. Since the c2-square is defended twice, considering
27...Bc2 as a candidate is the difficult part; after that, the variations are not so difficult to calculate.
 a) 27...Bg6 is slow by comparison, but still gains an advantage. For example: 28.gxf4 Qxf4
29.Qe2 Qxd2 30.Qxd2 Bxd2µ
 b) 27...Nh3+ 28.Bxh3 gxh3µ was the game, when White is not yet dead.
28.Nxc2 28.Qxc2 is mated most quickly by 28...Ne2+ (though 28...Nh3+ would get there
two moves more slowly). 28.Qxg4 must be met by: 28...Nh3+!–+  Otherwise White is better.
29.Qxh3 Qxf2+ 30.Kh1 Qxe1 White will lose masses of material, then get mated. For example:
31.Rf3 Be4 32.Nxe4 Rxf3 28...Nh3+ 29.Bxh3 Of course 29.Kh1 Nxf2+ is a winning fork.
29...Qxf2+ 30.Kh1 gxh3!–+  When playing 27...Bc2, it was essential to realize this position
is winning. The threat of mate on g2 leaves White no time to save the d2-knight. 31.Qg1 Qxd2
Black is only a pawn up, but it’s a forced mate. For example: 32.Ra2 Qe2 Threatening checks
on f3 or e4.

24.Rbe1!+– Preparing the queen check on h8 by covering the black king’s escape route. For
White, 24.Rbe1 is the right square and the right rook, though you need to see a few key lines to
understand why.
 In the game Carlsen tried to do it all with checks: 24.Qh8+? Ke7 25.Rfe1+ Be6 The position
was messy, but had he played 26.Qh4!?² then White would still be a touch better.
 Instead, the “wrong rook” move 24.Rfe1? allows 24...Be6² when, unlike the main line, White
cannot lift the e1-rook, as it would leave its colleague on b1 hanging.
 24...Rxe1 24...Be6 is refuted most simply by 25.Re3!+–  with the idea Nxe6+ ...fxe6, Rf3
skewering the queen (also winning, but in messier style, is 25.g4+– with the ideas 25...Qxg4+
26.Qxg4 Bxg4 27.Nh7+! and 25...Qg6 26.f4! threatening f4-f5). 25.Rxe1 Be6 26.Qh8+! 
Creating an annoying pin on the b8-knight. The second-best 26.f4± secures an advantage, but is
too much weaker than the text move to be worthy of any credit. 26...Ke7 27.h4!+– Finding this
slow move, defending the knight and creating luft, would be a brilliant achievement for a non-
computer. 27.Qxg7 is not such a bad move, but Black can fight on after: 27...Kd6! 28.h4± The
obvious 27.Nxe6? throws away all White’s advantage after: 27...fxe6 28.Qxg7+ Kd6= 27...Qd5
Trying to unpin the b8-knight. Unlike the 27.Qxg7 line above, 27...Kd6 no longer works for
Black: 28.Nxe6 (or the check on d8 first) 28...fxe6 29.Qd8+ (29.Rd1+ is similar) 29...Kc6
30.Qc8++– Black is busted after 30...Kb6 31.Rxe6+ or 30...Kd6 31.Rd1+ Ke5 32.Qb7 (or
many other 32nd moves). 28.Qxg7 28.c4+– also works. For example: 28...Qd4 29.Qh5 Qf6
30.Nxe6 fxe6 31.Qd5 is decisive. 28...Kd8 Or 28...Kd6 can be killed most swiftly by: 29.Nxe6!
(the obvious 29.h5 should win, just not at once) 29...fxe6 30.c4!+– For example: 30...Qxc4
31.Qg3+ Ke7 32.Rd1 And the attack wins far too much material. 29.h5+– The h-pawn is going
all the way.
